questions.q: How many bits of memory do 3 classical bits need, and how many possible configurations does that system have?
options: 3 bits of memory; 2^3 = 8 possible configurations, though the system is only ever in exactly one at a time
8 bits of memory; 3 possible configurations
3 bits of memory; 3 possible configurations, one per bit
2^3 = 8 bits of memory; 8 possible configurations, all occupied simultaneously
questions.explain: Storing 3 classical bits takes exactly 3 bits of memory. The state space those 3 bits can range over has 2^3 = 8 members (000 through 111), but at any instant the system occupies exactly one of those 8 configurations — memory cost and description cost both stay linear in n, even though the space of possibilities is exponential in n.

questions.q: How many complex amplitudes are needed to fully specify the general state of 3 qubits, and why?
options: 8, because the 3-qubit state vector lives in a 2^3-dimensional complex space with one amplitude per basis string (000 through 111)
3, one amplitude per qubit
6, two amplitudes per qubit for its 0 and 1 components
1, since the entire 3-qubit system collapses to a single combined amplitude
questions.explain: A general n-qubit state is a linear combination over all 2^n computational basis strings, each with its own complex amplitude. For n=3, that's 2^3 = 8 amplitudes (c_0 through c_7, one per 3-bit string), constrained so the sum of their squared magnitudes equals 1.

questions.q: In the worked 3-qubit uniform superposition example, each of the 8 amplitudes is 1/√8. What is the resulting probability of measuring any one specific basis state, and do all 8 probabilities sum to 1?
options: Each probability is (1/√8)^2 = 1/8 = 0.125, and 8 × 0.125 = 1, confirming correct normalization
Each probability is 1/√8 directly, and they sum to 8/√8
Each probability is 1/8, but they sum to 8 since there are 8 states
Each probability is 1, since every basis state is equally likely to be the true state before measurement
questions.explain: The Born rule says probability equals the squared magnitude of the amplitude: (1/√8)^2 = 1/8 exactly. Summing 1/8 across all 8 equally-likely outcomes gives exactly 1, which is required for a valid normalized state and was confirmed numerically in the lesson (8 × 0.125 = 0.9999999999999998, equal to 1 up to floating-point rounding).

questions.q: What is the core tension this lab identifies between representing and reading out an n-qubit system?
options: Representing the state needs resources that grow as 2^n, but a single measurement only ever yields exactly n classical bits, no matter how large the state vector is
Representing the state needs only n resources, but reading it out requires 2^n separate measurements
Both representing and reading out an n-qubit system scale linearly in n, identically to classical bits
Representing the state is impossible for any n greater than 1, so readout is the only well-defined operation
questions.explain: This is the exponential-representation / linear-readout gap: a general n-qubit state needs 2^n amplitudes to describe fully, but any single measurement collapses the system to one definite n-bit classical outcome — you never get more than n bits out of one measurement, regardless of how rich the underlying amplitude structure was.

questions.q: Why does this representation-vs-readout gap matter for topics later in this course, such as simulating quantum systems on classical computers?
options: Because a classical computer trying to track all 2^n amplitudes exactly hits the same exponential growth from the representation side, which is the structural reason quantum systems become hard to simulate classically as n grows
Because classical computers can already read out all 2^n amplitudes directly from a quantum system in one step, making simulation trivial
Because the gap only applies to quantum computers and has no bearing on classical simulation at all
Because simulating n qubits classically only ever requires n bits of memory, same as the qubits themselves
questions.explain: If fully describing an n-qubit state requires 2^n amplitudes, then a classical computer attempting to simulate that state exactly must also track on the order of 2^n numbers — the same exponential wall shows up from the simulation side. This is exactly the limitation explored later in the course under quantum simulation, and it's also the flip side of why quantum hardware can be powerful: it's natively working with that same exponential structure instead of simulating it.
